6.10.12 Assays for polymorphisms

Polymoφhisms represent differences in DNA sequence between members of the same species. Polymoφhisms include for example, single nucleotide polymoφhisms (SNPs), variations in Short Tandem Repeats (STRs), Restriction Fragment Length Polymoφhisms (RFLPs), insertions, deletions and rearrangements.

Well developed methods exist in the art for assaying polymoφhic and phenotypic differences between individuals by genetic mapping to characterize the genetic changes that give rise to phenotypic variation. These methods can be used, for example, to discover mutations responsible for genetic disease, to manipulate and breed useful traits in plants and animals, to discover elements in genetic pathways, to diagnose propensity towards disease, to determine and diagnose drug response, etc. (see for example, Stone et ah, 1999; Lebo et ah, 1998; Giordano et ah, 1998; Rothschild et ah, 1996; Blumenfeld et ah, 1995; Meyer et ah, 1997; Kamb, 1997; Skolnick et ah, 1997). Many phenotypic traits are multifactorial and methods are well known for using polymoφhisms to discover Quantitative Trait Loci (see for example Webb et ah, 1999; Helentjaris et ah, 1995; Dupuis et ah, 1999; Umari et ah, 1996; Lander et ah, 1986 & 1989). STRs are highly polymoφhic genetic elements and their use in genetic mapping is well known in the art, see for example Caskey et a (1994) and Polymeropoulos (1995). The utility of SNPs for genetic mapping has recently progressed considerably due to improvements in technology, in particular the ability to assay many different SNPs simultaneously by using for example oligonucleotide arrays. For representative examples see Nikiforov et a (1999); Shuber, A.P. (1996); Jakubowski et ah (1999); Cho et ah (1999); Brookes (1999); Kruglyak (1999); Sapolsky et a (1999); Xiong et a (1999); Wang et a (1998). Polymoφhisms are easily discovered by sequencing DNA from one or more individuals according to the methods described above and comparing the sequences to discover differences in homologous regions. Indeed, the sequencing invention can be used both as a means to discover new polymoφhisms and as a method to assay polymoφhisms for genetic mapping studies. Clearly any type of polymoφhism can be quickly assayed by sequencing the DNA (see e.g. Santamaria et ah, 1997).

To minimize the number of sequences needed to assay an individual, DNA may be enriched for polymoφhisms prior to the sequencing reaction. For example,
oo
Ostrander et a (1992) describe a method to enrich for STR sequences in a genomic library. For other examples see Kandpal et a (1994); Karagyozov et a (1993) and Paetkau (1999).

The physical mapping methods described above provide another means to discover and assay polymoφhic differences between individuals in a population. In most cases, differences in the landmarks between individuals represent differences in the nucleotide sequence. There are exceptions, for example differences in methylation patterns between individuals can be assayed by employing bisulfite-induced modifications prior to cloning the DNA whereby cytosine is converted to uracil, but 5- methylcytosine remains unchanged (see e.g., Frommer et ah, 1992).

A prefeπed landmark for assaying polymoφhisms is the restriction site. For example, assuming 0.1% of nucleotides are polymoφhic between two homologous chromosomes, then for any 6-base restriction site about 1 in 167 sites will be polymoφhic (i.e. one site will be cut by the restriction enzyme and one site cannot be cut). If we assume a genome size of 3x10 base pairs, then we can expect about (3xl0°746)/167 = -4400 polymoφhic restriction sites per assayed 6-base restriction enzyme. Of course, once polymoφhisms are discovered, they can be assayed in a population by other methods such as those mentioned above.
6.10.13 Assays for genomic alterations w ithin an individual

Changes can occur in the genome of an individual during the course of development or during the progression of disease. The result is variation between different populations of cells within the individual. This variation can be assayed using the parallel methods of this invention. Any change at the nucleotide level can be determined simply by sequencing the genomic DNA from different populations of cells using the parallel methods described above. For example, the sequence of DNA from cancerous tissue can be compared to the sequence of DNA from nearby normal tissue. Changes in the genome are known to occur during disease progression, and analysis at the sequence level can help to pinpoint those changes that contribute to the diseased state.

Genomic reaπangements can readily be assayed at a lower resolution by observing differences in the landmarks. In particular, changes in restriction site
patterns will occur not only as a result of single base changes, but also due to rearrangements at both a fine and gross level. The physical mapping methods described above typically yield information from a larger contiguous stretch of DNA than the sequencing methods. Thus fewer clones need to be analyzed to quickly "survey" the genomic DNA from, for example, a diseased tissue. Reaπangements discovered in this manner may represent changes that contribute to the diseased state.

I claim: 1. A parallel method for polynucleotide sequencing, comprising: a) preparing a library comprising a collection of two or more sample- tagged polynucleotide clones; b) carrying out a nucleic acid sequencing reaction on the library wherein a first sequencing primer binding site or no sequencing primer binding site is used to generate a plurality of tagged reaction products from the sample-tagged clones in the collection; c) separating the reaction products according to size; d) collecting fractions of the separated reaction products; e) amplifying the products collected in step (d) to generate tagged amplicons; f) hybridizing the tagged amplicons to an aπay comprising tag complements; and g) determining a plurality of polynucleotide sequences of the sample- tagged clones by detecting the hybridizations to deconvolute a plurality of sequence ladders for the sample-tagged clones in the collection. 2.
